The Sanskrit text below has been reconstructed primarily based on the three manuscripts listed in the abbreviations. Furthermore, the Derge edition of the Tibetan translation was consulted for sections containing transcribed Sanskrit, such as mantras or proper names, and the *Sādhanamālā* was consulted for the short passage that parallels one of the *sādhanas* of Bhūtaḍāmara (no. 264). App. 2.

The present edition is not a fully critical one, and several important points must be noted. First, minor amendments—primarily orthographic, though occasionally grammatical—have not been reported in the critical apparatus. Second, the edition follows manuscript G by default, failing to report variant readings unless the adopted reading originates from a manuscript other than G. Third, in instances where variants are reported, manuscript A served as the primary reference; manuscript B was consulted only when neither G nor A yielded a sensible reading, or when its proposed reading appeared particularly pertinent. Regarding the text cited in the lemmata, if the scribe’s corrections were involved, it always represents the *post correctionem* version. In cases where rectifying flawed grammar would necessitate arbitrary conjecture, the preferred course was to leave the source text unchanged.
approximately 3

Unlike manuscripts A and B, which were available in JPEG format, manuscript G was kindly provided by Dr. Péter-Dániel Szántó in the form of a transcript. This transcript included numerous minor emendations made by him (which almost invariably proved to be corroborated by other manuscripts). These emendations have likewise been adopted in this edition, without being reported in the critical apparatus. Any errors that occurred during the adaptation of the contents of G for the present edition are my own.

Of the three manuscripts, G appears to be the closest to the Tibetan translation, followed by A. These two manuscripts are the primary witnesses for the present edition. In general, when choosing between textual variants, we followed the Sanskrit source that corresponded with the Tibetan text.

Regarding the dates of the manuscripts, G is the oldest of the three. Its script (a variety of Māgadhī) indicates that it is likely pre-thirteenth century. Manuscript A contains a date in its colophon that assigns it to the mid-sixteenth century, while B is a relatively recent paper copy. App. 6.

In an effort to preserve some of the character of the language used in the transmission of the *Bhūtaḍāmara*—which is Classical Sanskrit with certain Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit influences and its own peculiarities—only limited editorial standardization has been applied, leaving a number of features intact. Thus, following the convention of the manuscripts, vowel sandhi has, for the most part, not been applied; for example, the Sanskrit absolutive is always written separately from the following word (*...gatvā aṣṭa-śataṃ japet*, rather than *...gatvāṣṭa-śataṃ japet*).
approximately 7

Spelling has been standardized throughout the text, but the application of *saṃdhi* rules has not. We made this choice to follow the conventions of ancient manuscript scribes, who applied *saṃdhi* with discretion. Their decision not to apply *saṃdhi* in specific instances appears to reflect an intention to clarify the text; therefore, our standardization would constitute an unnecessary and unhelpful intervention. Mantric syllables such as *oṃ* and *hūṃ* (that is, those ending in a nasal sound) are spelled throughout this edition with the *anunāsika* (ṃ) rather than the *anusvāra* (ṃ), regardless of the spelling found in the manuscripts.
approximately 8

The present edition is intended solely to accompany the English translation and does not claim to provide a definitive basis for further philological research. Any scholar intending to cite from this edition in an academic publication is advised to verify the cited text against the original manuscripts. Two of these manuscripts are available for free download from the Tokyo University Library (http://utlsktms.ioc.u-tokyo.ac.jp/utlsktms/syahonSearch.do); the third may become accessible through the Göttingen University Library database, should its manuscript collection be digitized as rumored.
approximately 9

The passage numbers (enclosed in double daṇḍas) correspond to the numbering provided for the respective sections in the English translation. For scholars wishing to consult the original manuscripts, the folio numbers for manuscripts G and A have been added in brackets. This format includes the siglum, the number, and either “r” or “v” to indicate the “recto” or “verso” side. For example, {A13r} denotes the recto side of the thirteenth folio of manuscript A. The location of each number in our edition corresponds to the beginning of the first line of a manuscript folio, occasionally following its first word.
Approximately 10.

Due to missing portions of the text in one of the sources for this edition—namely, Szántó’s transcript of manuscript G—there is a gap in the numbering of folios between {G9v} and {G11v}, as the precise location of the folio breaks could not be determined.

Now, therefore, in the *Bhūtaḍāmara-mahātantrarāja*, I shall proclaim the detailed procedure for the practice (*sādhana*) of all male and female spirits (*bhūta-bhūtinī*). Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Vajradhara, the Lord of the Three Worlds.

One should practice at a confluence of rivers, in a cremation ground, under a solitary tree, in a temple, or in the abode of Śrīvajradhara; in such places as these, one will achieve success in that very instant. If one does not succeed, the entire family and lineage of the *bhūtabhūtinī* shall perish.
Then Maheśvara Mahādeva, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, the Lord of Great Wrath, proclaim the mantra-words for the slaying of wicked spirits and Māras."
Then he gave a cry of approval to Maheśvara, Mahādeva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Mahādeva! This is well-spoken."
Then the Blessed One spoke the mantra syllables for the slaying of all spirits:
Oṃ vajrajvāle hana hana sarvabhūtān hūṃ phaṭ!

Then, as soon as this was spoken, numerous vajra-flames issued forth from the pores of Śrīvajradhara’s body. The bodies of all the Bhūtas and Bhūtinīs were withered away, and all the deities, including Śakra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest, were rendered lifeless.
Then all the Tathāgatas, with amazement, said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, excellent, Vajradhara, Great Lord of Wrath! In the future time, in the final age, you perform the subjugation of all male and female spirits.”
Then the Blessed One spoke again the mantra for summoning the consciousness of the deceased:
Oṃ vajrāyuṣe sara sara asmin.

Then, as soon as this was spoken, from the nose of the glorious Vajradhara there issued forth the Great Wind, the Reviver of the Dead. As soon as it had issued forth, it entered the bodies of all the female spirits (*bhūtinī*). As soon as it had entered, the female spirits rose up, trembling with great fear, and cried out:
"May the Blessed One protect us! May the Sugata protect us! May the Blessed One give his command!"
Then Aparājita, the lord of the great elements, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One within that great circle of the assembly, spoke to the Blessed One, the Lord of Great Wrath:
"O Lord of Wrath, Śrī Tribhuvanavijayī, may the Blessed One protect us! May the Sugata protect us!"
The Blessed One said:

"O noble ones, Lord of Beings! Having undertaken this, I shall grant the fulfillment of success for humans throughout the world-systems of the four continents. I shall grant the elixir of flavors, perfected substances, and the happiness of health to the humans of Jambudvīpa. I shall grant gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, rubies, sun-crystals, moon-crystals, garments, perfumes, and all desired foods. I shall become a servant to those who recite the wrathful mantras; I shall become their attendant. To those who recite the mantras of all the Tathāgatas, I shall provide great jewels, garments, perfumes, incense, flowers, and all other requisites, as well as every necessary substance, without fail. I shall ward off all fear of kings and enemies, and all fear of lions and tigers, and I shall provide every requisite without hindrance."

"O, O Aparājita, Lord of the Great Elements! Speak the truth, speak it again and again! I shall certainly grant success even to those who are lazy, ill-behaved, evildoers, and liars. If you do not grant success, I shall shatter your head with my great, irresistible vajra against the Vidyādharīs, Bhūtinīs, Nāginīs, Yakṣiṇīs, Śālabhañjikās, Kiṃnarīs, Mahoragīs, Garuḍīs, Piśācinīs, and Gandharvīs; I shall cast you into the eight great hells!"

All the Tathāgatas were filled with wonder and said this: "Excellent, excellent, Vajrapāṇi! Well spoken! For the benefit of human beings, may the Great Bodhisattva speak on this chapter of various kinds of extensive mudrās and mantras—[the chapter] of him whose power and prowess consist of unimpeded, perfected vigor; who is honored by all the gods; the great king of the three realms; the accomplisher of all the world-systems of the four continents; the turner of the wheel of all dharmas; and the destroyer of all suffering. May the Blessed One, the Great Wrathful King, the Lord of Great Wrath, speak!
Then Vajradhara, the Great Lord of Wrath, spoke again the mantra for reviving the dead:
Oṃ kaḍḍa kaḍḍa mṛtasaṃjīvāpaya hrīḥ āḥ.
Then, as soon as this had been spoken, all the deities, having lost consciousness, fell down; trembling with great fear, they rose up again.
Then Mahādeva said:
"May the Great Bodhisattva protect me!"
Then Vajradhara, the great Lord of Wrathful Deities, spoke these words:
"Do not fear, do not fear, O Lord of Beings! For the sake of your defeat, I shall bring all the gods under my control and effect the subjugation of all spirits."
Then all the *apsarases* said this to the Lord of the Vidyādharas:
"May the Blessed One protect us! May the glorious Vajradhara, the Great King, protect us!"

Then Vajradhara, the Great Lord of Wrath, spoke thus: "Accept these celestial nymphs! I shall perform service for the reciter of the Śrīvajradhara mantra; I shall give all manner of riches, such as silver, gold, pearls, lapis lazuli, rubies, and so forth."
Then, led by the Apsarases, all the daughters of the gods and the Yakṣiṇīs addressed him as follows:

"I die, I die, O Blessed One! May I become a servant to those who recite the mantra of the glorious Vajradhara; may we become attendants. If we do not become attendants to those who recite the wrathful mantras, then we shall be destroyers of all families and lineages. We shall be those who revile the true Dharma; we shall be censured by all the Tathāgatas. May the Blessed One shatter our heads with the Wrathful Vajra; shattered into a hundred pieces, we shall quickly die and enter the eight great hells."
Then the great bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi gave his approval to all the apsarases, divine maidens, nāginīs, and yakṣiṇīs:
“Excellent, excellent, O apsarases, divine maidens, nāginīs, and yakṣiṇīs! In the future time, in the final age, may you become attendants to those humans who recite the Tathāgata’s name.”

1.22 Now, therefore, the Bhūtarājas of the spirit-servants (bhūtaceṭaka), beginning with Aparājita, rose within the circle of their own assembly and, having bowed their heads at the feet of the glorious Vajradhara, the Great Lord of Wrath, offered their own heart-mantras:

Oṃ śrīmahābhūtakulasundari hūṃ | Oṃ śrīvijayasundari hrīḥ | Oṃ vimalasundari āḥ | Oṃ śrīratisundari vāḥ | Oṃ śrīmanoharasundari dhīḥ | Oṃ śrībhīṣaṇasundari iḥ | Oṃ śrīdhavalasundari maṃ | Oṃ śrīcakṣurmadhusundari bhīḥ |
Thus, these eight are the Queens of the Elements (bhūtarājñīs), celebrated by the word "Śrī."

Now follows the method of accomplishment: merely by reciting it, it bestows all success. Merely by uttering the name of the glorious Vajradhara, all spirits and elemental powers become his servants and handmaidens.
The Blessed One said:
"If you transgress the agreement, at the very moment of its transgression, I shall destroy the own family and lineage of all the female spirits of the bhūtas."
Then Aparājita, the lord of the great elements, spoke thus to the Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara:

"I abide by the commitment (*samaya*) of Mahādeva. I shall grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*) through the application of all worldly mantras and mudrās. By the mere recitation of the mantra of the glorious Vajradhara, we grant all accomplishments. If we do not grant them, we become destroyers of our own family and lineage; we become violators of the commitment within the teaching of all the Tathāgatas. The Blessed One will shatter our heads with his Wrathful Vajra. We shall die swiftly and enter the eight great hells.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme location for practice:
on a riverbank, in a cremation ground, or likewise in the house of Vajrapāṇi.
All the Bhūtabhūtis are accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
The place for the practice of the eight great elemental kings.
Now, I shall explain the eight mudrās for the accomplishment of prosperity:
having formed a firm fist with the left hand, one should extend the middle finger.
Having invoked her, the Pūjanī-mudrā is the means for accomplishing the supreme family.
With the hands joined in a mutual fist, one should extend the index fingers;
Bhūtabhūtinī, who protects her own pledge, is accomplished at that very moment.
Having formed a firm fist with the left hand, one should extend the little finger;
this is the *sāṃnidhyakaraṇa* mudrā, which follows all beings.
Extending the left hand, forming the *tarjanī* finger into a coil,
and pressing it down with the thumb (*jyeṣṭhā*) and the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*), this is the mudrā that brings all beings under one's control.
Forming a fist with the left hand, one should extend the ring finger;
this attracts all female spirits and wards off all obstacles.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the thumb and the index finger;
this is the Bhūtiny-abhimukhī mudrā, which causes the destruction of all that is evil.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the little finger;
this is the Bhūtinī-samayamudrā, which accomplishes all things and performs all rites.

Having formed the *khaṭaka* with both hands, place them separately on the right hip; having positioned the left hand resting upon the right, this is the supreme heart-mudrā of the pledge of all *bhūtinīs*.
As soon as these are bound, the Bhūtinīs quickly arrive. If they do not arrive quickly, they burst in the eyes, wither, or die.
Then the glorious Vajradhara, the great lord of wrathful deities, spoke this:
"If the female spirits (*bhūtinī*) transgress their respective commitments (*samaya*), one should draw them in with this [mantra] accompanied by wrath and recite it eight hundred times."
Oṃ kaḍḍa kaḍḍa sruṃ hrīḥ [Name]bhūtinī hūṃ phaṭ!
With this [mantra], accompanied by anger, one should recite it one hundred and eight times. He will come quickly. If he does not come quickly, his eyes and head will burst, wither, or he will die.
Now follows the method of accomplishment:

having gone to the confluence of two rivers, one should draw a mandala with sandalwood paste and offer a profusion of flowers. One should burn guggulu incense and recite the mantra eight thousand times; then one becomes accomplished. Furthermore, one should recite it one thousand times at night; she will certainly come. When she has arrived, she should be enjoyed as a wife. Having left a hundred palas of gold upon the bed, she departs at dawn. In this manner, day by day, within a month, success is certain.

Having gone to a riverbank and having drawn a mandala with sandalwood paste, one should cause an offering of curd-rice to be presented. One should recite the mantra eight thousand times for seven days. On the seventh day, she will certainly arrive. When she has arrived, an *argha* offering of sandalwood water should be given; she will become pleased. She will say, "Child, what must I do? The practitioner should say, "Give me a kingdom. She will grant a kingdom; she will also protect the realm and provide garments, ornaments, food, and other necessities.

Having gone to the abode of Śrīvajradhara, one should offer *karavīra* flowers and burn *guggulu* incense. One should recite the mantra eight thousand times; she becomes accomplished. Furthermore, one should recite it a thousand times during the night; she will certainly come. To her when she has arrived, one should offer a seat of flowers and say, "Welcome. She becomes one's wife. She bestows divine elixirs (*rasāyana*) and perfected substances. She strikes down all enemies. Having placed [the practitioner] upon her back, she leads even him to heaven. One lives for ten thousand years.

Having gone to a riverbank, one should draw a mandala with sandalwood paste and offer white flowers, white perfumes, and incense of *turuṣka*. One should recite the mantra eight thousand times; then it becomes effective. One should recite again at night; she will certainly come. When she has arrived, an offering (*argha*) should be given with flowers and water. She should be addressed: "Become my sister. She then bestows elixirs, alchemical preparations, and perfected substances; she even brings and gives a woman from as far as a thousand *yojanas* away.

Having gone to an empty temple, having performed the offering and worship as prescribed, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; success is achieved. Again, at night, having offered the *bali* oblation, one should recite it a thousand times. She will certainly come. Once she has arrived, she should be enjoyed; she becomes one's wife. Day by day she gives a thousand *dīnāras*. Placing [the practitioner] upon her back, she carries him even to Mount Sumeru. Furthermore, she grants the entire kingdom or a royal maiden. One lives for five thousand years. When one dies, one is reborn into a royal family.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.43: *parasmaipadānām ṇalatususthalathusaṇalvamāḥ* (For the parasmaipada endings, there are substituted respectively: ṇal, atus, us, tha, athus, a, ṇal, va, and mas.)

Having gone to a confluence of rivers, one should offer a *karavīra* flower with meat as food. One should fumigate with *guggulu* incense and recite the mantra eight thousand times; then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). Again, at night, having performed a magnificent worship and lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite it a thousand times. She arrives surrounded by five hundred attendants. Once she has arrived, she should be enjoyed in silence. She becomes one’s wife. If one neglects her, then she perishes. Carrying her on one’s back day after day, she leads even to heaven. Furthermore, one becomes a king and lives for five thousand years. When one dies, one is reborn in a royal family.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.44: *pratyayaḥ* (an affix).

Having gone to the bank of a river, one should draw a mandala with saffron, offer agallochum incense, and cause the bali offering as prescribed to be given. One should recite the mantra eight thousand times; success will then occur. Furthermore, having performed a grand worship at night, one should recite it a thousand times. She comes of her own accord, creating a great radiance. An offering (argha) should be presented with sandalwood water. Then she becomes pleased and asks, "Child, what must I do for you? The practitioner should say, "Be my mother. She protects him like a mother, along with five hundred attendants, and provides food, ornaments, and garments every day. He lives for ten thousand years, and when he dies, he is reborn in a brahmin family.

At the confluence of rivers, having performed a grand offering of oblations (*balipūjā*) and lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night. Then, at the time of midnight, she arrives, creating a great radiance, and asks: "Child, what must I do? The practitioner should say: "Give me a kingdom. Day after day, she gives a hundred thousand *dīnāra* coins. One lives for ten thousand years. When one dies, one is reborn as a universal monarch (*sārvabhūmika-rāja*).
The eight great elemental queens are completed.

Then Mahābhūtinī, who enters the cremation ground, arose, bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, and gave him her own heart-mantra:
Oṃ hrīḥ hūṃ aḥ. This is the supreme heart-mantra.

Oṃ hūṃ kaḍḍa kaḍḍa! Observe the pledge of all the *bhūtinīs*! Strike! Strike! Bind! Bind! Attack! Attack! O you, O Great Fierce One, dweller in the cremation ground, come quickly! Dhruṃ phaṭ! This is the mantra for summoning the *bhūtinīs* who dwell in the cremation ground.

Oṃ dhūna dhūna vidhūna vidhūna cala cala cālaya cālaya praviśa praviśa hana hana tiṣṭha tiṣṭha samayam anupālaya bho bho śmaśānapraveśini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the samaya-mantra of Śmaśānapraveśinī, the mistress of all bhūtas.

Oṃ cala cala dhaka dhaka, O you of great elements, who are fond of being favorable to practitioners! Move, move! Spread forth, spread forth! Draw near, draw near! Speak, speak! Break, break! Raṅga raṅga! Seize, seize! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hrīḥ svāhā! Daṃṣṭrākarālī!
Oṃ, O Ghoramukhī, dweller in the cremation ground, favorable to practitioners, bestower of unimpeded siddhis! Oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ, homage, svāhā! Ghoramukhī.

Oṃ! O Jarjaramukhī! O Cira! Cira! O you who possess the power of thought! O you who cause fear to all enemies! Strike! Strike! Burn! Burn! Cook! Cook! Slay! Slay! O you who bring about the destruction of untimely death for me! O you who cause fear to all *nāgas*! O you who laugh with loud, boisterous laughter! O Sovereign Lady of all beings! Thā thā thā thā! Dhā dhā dhā dhā! Oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ svāhā! Jarjaramukhī!

Oṃ! O lotus-eyed one, compassionate toward humanity, destroyer of all suffering, beloved of practitioners, victory, victory, O you of divine form! Hrīḥ! Seize, seize! Jaḥ jaḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Homage! Svāhā! This is the mantra of Kamalalocanī.
Oṃ! O you of hideous face, with fangs most terrible and flaming eyes, who causes fear to all yakṣas! Run, run! Go, go! O practitioner, what do you command? Svāhā! Vikaṭamukhī!

Oṃ dhudhurī! O you who devour karma, kaha kaha! Shake, shake! You who are worshipped by the great asuras, cut, cut! Pierce, pierce! O great devourers of karma, bho bho! O practitioner, what shall I do? Hrīḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! Dhudhurī!

Ap 2.12: The mantra for entering the eight great cremation grounds.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the characteristics of the mudrā for entering the Great Cremation Ground (mahāśmaśānapraveśinīmudrā).
Having formed two fists with the hands, one should extend the two index fingers. This is the Bhūtinī Samaya-mudrā. With this very Samaya-mudrā, one should perform the invocation.
There are eight mudrās of the piśācīs who enter the great cremation grounds.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the index finger; this is the Ghoramukhī mudrā.
Having formed the mutual fist, one should interlace the two little fingers and extend the two index fingers; one should apply this to the region of the mouth. This is the Daṃṣṭrākarālī mudrā.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the middle finger; this is the Jarjarī mudrā.
In this very same mudrā, the middle fingers are bent and the ring fingers are extended; this is the Kamalalocanī mudrā.
Into this very same mudrā, one should insert the ring finger and extend the little finger; this is the Vikaṭamukhī mudrā.
Having formed a fist with the right hand, one should extend the index finger; this is the *dhudhurī* mudrā.
Having bent the index finger of this very same mudrā, one should extend the middle finger. This is the Vidyutkarālī mudrā.
Having formed a fist with the right hand, one should extend the little finger; this is the Saumyamukhī mudrā.
The Extensive Tantra on the Ritual for the Characteristics of the Mudrās of the Bhūtinīs Who Enter the Eight Great Cremation Grounds.
Chapter 3:
On the Refutation of the Self (Ātmavādapratiṣedha) A3.1. The Refutation of the Self as a Substance (Dravyātmavādapratiṣedha)
Now, therefore, in the *Bhūtaḍāmara-mahātantrarāja*, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the accomplishment of the eight Bhūtinīs who enter the great cremation grounds.
3.2 For the benefit of the poor, this is the supreme means of employing female servants.

Having gone to a cremation ground, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Thereafter, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*).

On the fourth night, having gone to a cremation ground, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *khadira* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, ghee, and clarified butter. Thereupon, a female spirit who dwells in the cremation ground will quickly arrive. She becomes a servant and performs tasks such as clearing fields, building fences, and agricultural work; she gives one *dīnāra* every day, day after day.

At night, having gone to the field enclosure, one should worship according to the prescribed rite for fish and meat; having recited the mantra twenty-one times as instructed, the Karmapiśācī performs the activities as described.

At night, having gone to a cremation ground, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times. Then Karmapiśācībhūtinī will quickly arrive in a gentle form. She becomes a servant and performs household tasks, speech-acts, and formidable rites, and so forth.

At night, having gone to a cremation ground, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times. Then Karmapiśācībhūtinī, surrounded by a retinue of a hundred, will quickly arrive. When she has arrived, one should offer a blood sacrifice according to the ritual for fish and meat. She becomes pleased and performs the tasks of a servant-maid (*ceṭī*). Day after day, she gives a pair of garments, one *dīnāra*, food, and ornaments to five people including herself. She even brings celestial women from as far as a hundred *yojanas* and gives them [to the practitioner]. In short, she performs the tasks of a servant-maid for as long as one lives.
In the *Bhūtaḍāmaramahātantra*, this is the extensive tantra on the ritual procedures for the Karmapiśācīs.

Oṃ bhū jvala hūṃ phaṭ! Mahākātyāyanī!

Now, therefore, follows the detailed procedure for the characteristics of the mudrās in the *Bhūtaḍāmara-mahātantrarāja*.
Having interlaced the fingers with one another, one should extend both index fingers and make them like needles; this is the *padmāsana* mudrā.
Having formed a mutual fist, one should encircle the two index fingers; this is the Great Mudrā for the Possession by Wrath. It causes the three worlds to be possessed in an instant.
Now, there are the six-limbed mudrās.
Having formed fists with the hands, one should extend the two middle fingers; this is the *śiromudrā* (head mudrā).
Inserting the two middle fingers of this very same mudrā and making the index fingers into needles constitutes the *śikhā* mudrā.
With this very mudrā, one should join the two thumbs at the sides—the right thumb with the right eye and the left thumb with the left eye. This is the Netra-mudrā (Eye Mudrā).
Having formed a mutual fist, one should wrap the two little fingers and extend the index fingers; this is the heart mudrā.
By forming the index finger into a ring with this very same mudrā, it becomes the armor mudrā (kavaca-mudrā).
By extending the index finger of this very same mudrā, it becomes the *astramudrā*.
Having placed the hands with palms facing upward, with the index fingers on the sides, this is the *arghamudrā*.
Having formed the mutual fist, one should extend the two thumbs; this is the Ākṣepa mudrā.

Having formed mutual fists and extended the respective left index fingers, one should place them at the base of the arms. Pressing the nail of the little finger with the right thumb, one should extend the remaining fingers. One should cast [the mudrā] with the base of the right arm. This is the Diśābandha-mudrā (Direction-Binding Mudrā).
Now follows the Mahādeva-mudrā:
having formed the añjali with palms facing upward, one should bend the index and ring fingers. This is the Bhagna-mudrā of Rudra.
Having placed the palms facing upward, one should encircle and bend the two index fingers; this is the conch mudrā of Nārāyaṇa.
Interlacing the fingers of both hands and extending the little fingers constitutes the water-pot mudrā of Prajāpati.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the middle finger; this is the Krauñcamathanaśakti mudrā.

Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the index and middle fingers; then, bending the index finger, one should hold it against the middle joint of the middle finger. This is the Gaṇapati-paraśu-mudrā (the axe-gesture of Gaṇapati).

Having made the palms open and joined, one should form the *svastika* there. Having bent the left little finger, one should place it upon the tip of the thumb; likewise, the right thumb [should be placed] upon the tip of the left thumb. This is the *āditya-ratha-mudrā*.
Extending the right hand and bending the index and ring fingers forms the Rāhu-mudrā.

Having formed the right hand in the shape of a dancer (*naṭya*) and placing it upon the head, one should form a fist with the left hand and extend the index and middle fingers. With the thumb, one should draw in the little finger and ring finger in the manner of a dancer. This is the *Narteśvara-mudrā*.
Having formed fists with each other, one should wrap the little fingers separately; this is the mudrā of Candra.
Now follows the mudrā of the goddess Umā:
having displayed both hands in the form of a serpent’s hood, one should place them upon the head.
Now follows the definition of the mudrās of the Śrī Devī:
one should cast the joined palms together (sampuṭāñjali) toward the region of space.

Now follows the mudrā of the goddess Śasī: having formed two fists with the hands, one should wrap the index fingers; then, in the manner of the flame of a remaining lamp, one should rotate them through the application of dance.

Now follows the Ratnabhūṣaṇī mudrā: having formed two fists with the hands, one should extend both index fingers. Placing the index fingers in the form of jewels at the region of the forehead, bound as if by a garland—this is the Ratnabhūṣaṇī mudrā. The mantra is: Oṃ ratnaśriye svāhā.
Now follows the mudrā of Sarasvatī:
having interlaced the fingers with one another, one should extend the two index fingers and place them at the mouth.
Now follows the mudrā of Tilottamā:
having interlaced the fingers with one another, one should hold the index fingers at the head.
Now follows the mudrā of Rambhā:
one should place the hands against each other in the shape of a cross at the heart.
Now follows the mudrā of Sarvayakṣeśvarīsurasundarī: having formed two fists with the hands, one should extend both little fingers and form them into little-finger earrings (*kaniṣṭhā-kuṇḍalī*).
Now follows the Bhūtinī mudrā: having formed two fists with the hands, one should interlace the two little fingers and form loops with the two index fingers.
Now follows the mudrā of Bhūtarājñī, the Sovereign of All Beings:
having formed two fists with the hands, one should interlace the two index fingers.
There are eight mudrās of prosperity.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the goddess Umā: having stepped upon the goddess Umā with his left foot, he should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the accomplishment that is difficult to surpass, which is exceedingly fierce and most terrible, and which accomplishes all aims.

Having gone to a solitary linga and having stepped upon the linga with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. Then Mahādeva arrives. If he does not arrive, one dies at that very moment.

Having stepped upon Nārāyaṇa with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. He will come quickly. If he does not come, his head will split open and he will die; Nārāyaṇa will become subject to him and will serve as his servant.

Having stepped upon Brahmā with his left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. He will arrive quickly; if he does not come, he will wither or die, and he will become a servant.

Having stepped upon Śakra with the left foot, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times for seven days. He will certainly come; Śakra becomes his servant. He brings Urvaśī and gives her [to him]. If he does not come, [the practitioner’s] head bursts, shattering into a hundred pieces, and his entire family and lineage perishes.

Having stepped upon the boy with his left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. He will quickly arrive; the boy becomes a servant, and all the Kumāra-grahas become attendants. One can cause such-and-such a person to live, and one can cause such-and-such a person to die.

Having stepped upon Gaṇapati with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. He will arrive quickly; if he does not come, he dies. All the Vināyakas become his servants.
Having stepped upon the sun with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days; he will arrive quickly and bestow sovereignty.

Having stepped upon the moon with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. The moon will quickly arrive; it bestows a hundred palas of gold, and the moon becomes subject to one's control.

Having stepped upon Bhairava with his left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. Then, at night, having performed a grand worship, having offered incense of *mahāmāṃsa*, having presented an offering of *mahāmāṃsa*, and having lit a lamp with great oil, he again lets out a great roar at the time of midnight. He rises with a loud, boisterous laugh and says, "O man, I shall devour you! One must not be afraid. If fear should ever arise, one should utter the syllable *HŪṂ*; he will become composed. Bhairava becomes subject to one's will; he bestows sovereignty over the triple world. By the mere utterance of *HŪṂ*, one destroys all worldly deities.

Having stepped upon Narteśvara with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. At that very moment, he arrives; he becomes a servant. If he does not come, he dies.

Having stepped upon Mahākāla with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. He arrives together with his retinue and attendants. If he does not arrive, he dies at that very moment. And Mahākāla becomes a servant.

Having gone to the temple of Caturmūrtīśvara, one should step upon it with the left foot and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for seven days. He arrives accompanied by his retinue and attendants. If he does not come, the practitioner dies. He becomes an attendant in every possible way; carrying one on his back, he even leads one to heaven. He brings and gives one Ūrvaśī, and he bestows divine elixirs and rejuvenators.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Lord of Wrathful Deities, the Glorious Vajradhara.

Now, therefore, in this *Ḍāmaramahātantrarāja*, which is the supreme secret among secrets, I shall proclaim the detailed procedure for the practice (*sādhana*) of the *Bhūtinī* [goddess], as spoken by Krodha himself for the benefit of the poor and for the attainment of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
For example: there are names of female spirits (bhūtinī), such as Vibhūṣaṇī, Kuṇḍalahāriṇī, Siṃhārī, Hāsinī, Naṭī, Rati, Kāmeśvarī, and Devī.
In brief, there are eight means for accomplishing prosperity: a wife, a mother, and a sister; [and likewise, a daughter-in-law, a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, and a niece].
Now follows the ritual procedure for the ornamentation.

Having gone to a *campaka* tree, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for three days at night. At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed a grand worship and offered *guggulu* incense, one should continue the recitation. Then, at midnight, Vibhūṣaṇī will certainly arrive. When she has arrived, an offering (*argha*) of sandalwood water should be given; she will become pleased. She may become a mother, a sister, or a wife. If she becomes a mother, she provides a retinue of eight hundred and bestows garments, ornaments, food, and so forth. If she becomes a wife, she gives a thousand *dīnāras*, as well as elixirs and alchemy (*rasāyana*). If she becomes a sister, she brings a celestial woman even from a thousand *yojanas* away and gives her; she also bestows divine elixirs, alchemy, and divine treasures.
Now follows the ritual procedure for Kuṇḍalahāriṇī.

Having gone to a cremation ground at night, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. At the conclusion of the recitation, Kuṇḍalahāriṇī Bhūtinī will certainly arrive. When she has arrived, an offering (argha) of blood should be presented; she will then be pleased. The practitioner should say, "Be my mother! and she will protect him like a mother.
Now follows the ritual procedure for Siṃhārī.

Having gone to a solitary shrine at night, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. The goddess herself will arrive and say, "O practitioner, what shall I do? Now follows the means for the attainment of laughter.

These must be spent entirely without remainder; if one keeps anything back, she will no longer appear. At night, a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*) appears.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the Naṭī.

At dawn, she will certainly arrive. Standing before one with a slight smile, she should be embraced and kissed; she should be enjoyed in silence. She becomes accomplished (siddha). Having gone to the confluence of rivers, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. No specific lunar day (*tithi*), nor constellation (*nakṣatra*), nor fasting is prescribed. Having gone to the summit of a mountain, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; then one should recite it again at night. Thereupon, she will certainly arrive at midnight. She becomes one's wife; she gives a hundred thousand *dīnāras* every day. Placing [the practitioner] upon her back, she carries him even across the four continents. She bestows elixirs, rejuvenators, and perfected substances.

Having gone to a temple of the deity, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for one month. Then, at the end of the month on the full moon day, one should recite it during the middle of the night. Thereupon, at midnight, she will certainly arrive accompanied by the sound of anklets. When she has arrived, one should offer her a seat of flowers and say, "Welcome, O Goddess! She will reply, "Lord, what do you command? The practitioner should say, "Become my wife. She performs the duties of a wife; she grants divine desires and lives for a thousand years.

15.11 Now follows the ritual procedure for Rambhā. Beginning on the first day of the lunar fortnight, having performed worship, having drawn a mandala with sandalwood paste, and having offered guggulu incense, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times at the three junctions of the day. Then, on the full moon day, having performed a great worship, one should recite throughout the entire night. At dawn, she will certainly arrive. If she does not come, [the practitioner] dies. She becomes his wife; she bestows elixirs and rejuvenators. She may be enjoyed as one desires. One lives for ten thousand years. When one dies, one is reborn in a royal family.
Now follows the means for attaining Urvaśī.

Having gone to a temple at night and offered sandalwood incense, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for one month. At the end of the month, having performed worship according to one's means, one should recite throughout the entire night. In the morning, she quickly arrives. To her who has arrived, one should offer a seat of flowers and say, "Welcome. She will ask, "O practitioner, what do you command? The practitioner should say, "Become my wife. She gives elixirs and alchemy; she gives perfected substances. One must avoid approaching the wives of others. One lives for five thousand years.
Now follows the sādhana of Śrībhūṣaṇī.

Having purified oneself at night while alone, one should draw Śrībhūṣaṇī on birch bark with saffron, offer incense of sandalwood, and recite the mantra for one month. At the end of the month, having performed a grand worship, one should continue reciting until midnight. Then, at midnight, she will certainly arrive. Once she has arrived, she should be quickly gratified; being pleased, she grants silver, gold, pearls, and the like. Day by day, she provides desired food and bestows elixirs and rejuvenating potions.

17.2 There follows the detailed procedure for the accomplishment of the eight yakṣiṇīs.

Having gone to the house of Vajrapāṇi and offered guggulu incense, one should recite the mantra a thousand times during the three junctions of the day. Within a month, she will certainly come. When she has arrived, an offering (argha) should be presented with sandalwood water. She performs the roles of mother, wife, and sister. If she is the mother, one must not harbor corrupt thoughts toward her. She gives elixirs and alchemy (rasāyana) every day; she gives a hundred thousand dīnāras. If she is the sister, she gives perfected substances, elixirs, and alchemy; having brought a divine celestial maiden, she gives her [to the practitioner]. She speaks of the past, future, and present. If she is the wife, she fulfills all desires, and one becomes a great lord of wealth.
Now follows the ritual procedure for Manohārī.

Having gone to the bank of a river, having prepared a mandala with sandalwood and performed a great worship, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times. One should fumigate it with agallochum incense. One should recite it ten thousand times for seven days. On the seventh day, having performed a magnificent worship, one should recite it throughout the entire night. Then, at midnight, she will certainly arrive. If she does not come, then one dies. She says, "Give me your command. The practitioner should say, "Become our servant. She maintains a retinue of eight hundred. She gives one hundred dīnāras every day as a certainty. That must be spent without remainder; if one sets aside anything, she will no longer appear.

17.4 Now follows the ritual for Kanakavatī. Having gone to a *vaṭa* tree, one should offer liquor according to the procedure for fish and meat. One should drink it oneself and then offer the remains as an oblation (*argha*). One should recite the mantra one thousand times. Thus, one should perform the practice at night on the seventh day. One should continue reciting until midnight, when she herself will arrive, adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by eight hundred attendants. When she has arrived, she should be enjoyed; she becomes one’s wife. She provides clothing, ornaments, food, and so forth for twelve people every day, and she gives eight *dīnāra*s.
Now follows the sādhana of Kāmeśvarī.

Having drawn an image on birch bark with yellow pigment (gorocanā), one should ascend a bed alone and recite [the mantra] one thousand times. Then, at the end of the month, having performed a grand worship and lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite while observing silence. Thereupon, she certainly arrives at midnight. Once arrived, she grants desires and becomes one's wife. Leaving her divine ornaments upon the bed, she departs at dawn. One must avoid approaching the wives of others; otherwise, one will perish.
Now follows the means for achieving pleasure.

A young girl, golden-colored, adorned with all ornaments, and holding a blue lotus in her hand, should be painted on a cloth. One should worship her with *jāti* flowers, offer *guggulu* incense, and recite the mantra eight thousand times for one month. At the end of the month, having performed worship according to one's means and lit a lamp of clarified butter, one should continue reciting until midnight, at which time she comes of her own accord. When she has arrived, she should be approached in silence; thus she becomes a wife. She protects the practitioner along with his retinue, provides divine and desirable foods, and bestows elixirs and rejuvenators worth twenty-five *dīnāras*.
Now follows the ritual for the Padminī.

Having prepared a mandala with sandalwood paste in the head-region of one’s own house and offered guggulu incense, one should recite the mantra one thousand times for one month. Then, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to one’s means, one should recite it until midnight; she will certainly arrive. Once arrived, she should be enjoyed. She becomes a wife who grants divine pleasures; she bestows elixirs and rejuvenators, and she provides perfected substances.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the Naṭī.

One should practice beneath an *aśoka* tree. Having offered incense, flowers, and perfumes while subsisting on meat, one should recite the mantra one thousand times. Within a month, she will certainly come. When she has arrived, she becomes either a mother, a sister, or a wife—in brief, whichever she is. If she is a mother, she gives desired food, a pair of garments, a hundred *pala* of gold, and elixirs of mercury. If she is a sister, she brings a celestial woman even from a thousand *yojanas* away and gives her; she also provides garments, ornaments, desired foods, and elixirs of mercury. If she is a wife, she gives divine elixirs of mercury and bestows eight *dīnāras*.
Now follows the practice for one who is enamored.

Having drawn the Yakṣiṇī with saffron on a birch-bark leaf, one should then recite the mantra three times a day for one month, beginning from the first lunar day, according to the ritual of perfumes, flowers, and lamps. Then, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to one’s means and lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite throughout the entire night. Thereupon, at dawn, she will certainly arrive. Once arrived, she grants all desires; she becomes one's wife. She bestows divine elixirs and rejuvenators, gives a thousand dīnāras, and one lives for thousands of years.

having formed two fists with the hands, one should interlace the two little fingers. Extending the two index fingers, one should bend them. This is the unimpeded hook-mudrā of the Wrathful One. By means of this king of mudrās, one may even summon the three worlds.
Now follows the characteristic of the Yakṣiṇī mudrā:

Having placed the palms of the hands together as even as possible, with the middle fingers reversed, the ring fingers should be placed horizontally on the outside; the index fingers are joined, and the little fingers are positioned within the hollow. Having gone to a Nāga abode, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. A Nāga maiden will quickly arrive. Forming a fist with the right hand and placing it at the mouth, one should extend the middle finger. This is the lamp mudrā.

23.3 Now follows the method for subduing the unconquerable:

Standing before a *caitya*, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times over seven days and nights. On the seventh day, having performed a grand worship, one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*). Having offered *guggulu* incense, one should continue the recitation. At the conclusion of the recitation, [the deity] will certainly arrive and say: "O practitioner, what must I do? One should reply: "Become my servant! [The deity] will then carry one upon its back and lead one even to the four continents; furthermore, it bestows a kingdom, and one lives for a thousand years.
Now follows the means for fulfillment (pūraṇasādhana).

Having gone to the abode of Vajradhara, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. On the seventh day, having performed a magnificent worship, one should cause white rice and curd to be offered as prescribed. One should continue reciting until midnight. Then, at midnight, he will certainly arrive. An offering (*argha*) of flowers should be presented; he becomes pleased and grants a kingdom. He fulfills all hopes, and one lives for thousands of years. For as long as one lives, he performs the tasks of a servant. He revives such-and-such a person and kills such-and-such a person; he does everything.
Now follows the means for filling [the vessel].

One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times before a shrine containing relics (*sadhātucaitya*). Thus, the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Then, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to one’s means, one should recite until midnight. Then, at midnight, he arrives swiftly; having arrived, he stands before [the practitioner] and says, "O child, what must I do? The practitioner should say, "Become my servant. From that time forth, he performs the duties of a servant. He brings and gives a divine yakṣa maiden; he reveals all hidden treasures (*nidhāna*); he provides divine, desirable food. Every day he gives a pair of garments or five *dīnāras*. One lives for five hundred years.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the Lord of the Cremation Ground.

Having gone to a cremation ground at night, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for seven days. On the seventh day, one should offer the prescribed oblation of fish, meat, sesame, *jambūtika*, white rice, curd, molasses, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). While burning *guggulu* incense, one should continue reciting until midnight. Then, a sound of "hā hā" will be heard. One must not be afraid; he arrives surrounded by his retinue. When he has arrived, one should present the offering (*bali*); he becomes pleased and becomes a servant to all beings. Day after day, he gives eight *dīnāras*. He causes all enemies to be destroyed, and one lives for a thousand years.
Now follows the sādhanā of Kuleśvara.

Having gone to a temple of the deities, having offered red perfumes, red flowers, and guggulu incense, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. Thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at night, having offered fish, meat, sesame, *jambūtika*, and red food according to the ritual procedure, and having offered turuṣka incense, one should recite until midnight. One of terrifying appearance, blazing intensely, will arrive. One must not be afraid of him. He will say, "Child, what shall I do? The practitioner should say, "Become my servant. As long as he lives, he performs the duties of a servant; he gives five *dīnāras* three times a day, provides divine and desirable food, and [the practitioner] lives for five hundred years.
Now follows the ritual procedure for Bhūteśvara.

Having gone to a solitary *liṅga*, one should remain alone for three days and nights, offering blood, rice, fish, meat, sesame, and *jambūtika*. One should fumigate with goat meat and *guggulu* incense along with honey. One should recite the mantra eight thousand times. On the first day, one sees him in a dream; on the second day, he comes quickly of his own accord and stands before one. He asks, "What should I do? The practitioner should say, "Become my servant. He becomes constantly obedient. He brings down an *apsaras* and gives her [to the practitioner]. He speaks of the past, future, and present. He provides clothing, ornaments, and desired food. He causes one to live for three hundred years.
Now, this is the supreme means for accomplishing the *kiṃkara*.

Having gone to the abode of Vajradhara, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for seven days on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. Thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Then, having offered incense of *guggulu*, seated upon a cushion of *kuśa* grass with white rice, ghee, and milk-rice, and having lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite during the night until midnight; then the servant (*kiṃkara*) will come of his own accord. To him who has arrived, an offering (*argha*) should be given with white sandalwood paste. He becomes pleased and says, "O practitioner, what must I do? The practitioner should say, "Become our servant. From that time forward, he performs the tasks of a servant and provides divine, desirable food. Carrying one upon his back, he even leads one to heaven; furthermore, he bestows a kingdom and causes one to live for five thousand years.

Now, therefore, in the *Bhūtaḍāmara-mahātantrarāja*, follows the description of the mudrās of the eight spirits (*bhūtas*).
One should interlace the fingers with one another, extend the two middle fingers, and hold them in the shape of a needle. This is the mudrā of the Great King Aparājita.
Having inserted the two middle fingers of this very same mudrā and extended the index fingers, one should bend them; this is the mudrā of Ajita.
By making the index finger of this very same mudrā into a loop and extending the little fingers separately, one has the mudrā of Pūraṇa.

Making the little finger of this very same mudrā into a needle is the mudrā of the Lord of the Cremation Ground.

Having formed the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed-palms gesture), one should bend the two index fingers; this is the mudrā of the Supreme Servant (*Kiṃkara*).

ap26. Chapter A26 ap26.1 The Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to remove all the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage from this great earth, and having done so, were to carry them away on the tip of a blade of kusa grass, thinking: ‘This is the footprint of the elephant, this is the footprint of the horse, this is the footprint of the ox. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would he be able to distinguish the footprints of those animals by their size? “Yes, venerable sir. “I say, bhikkhus, that among the footprints of living beings, the footprint of the elephant is the foremost, the greatest, and the most preeminent. So too, bhikkhus, among wholesome qualities, the noble eightfold path is the foremost, the greatest, and the most preeminent. And what, bhikkhus, is the noble eightfold path? It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the noble eightfold path, which I say is the foremost, the greatest, and the most preeminent among wholesome qualities. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, how is it that the noble eightfold path is the foremost, the greatest, and the most preeminent among wholesome qualities? “It is, bhikkhu, because this noble eightfold path leads to the complete destruction of suffering. That is why, bhikkhu, the noble eightfold path is the foremost, the greatest, and the most preeminent among wholesome qualities. When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, how does the noble eightfold path lead to the complete destruction of suffering? “It is, bhikkhu, because this noble eightfold path, when developed and cultivated, leads to the complete destruction of suffering. That is why, bhikkhu, the noble eightfold path leads to the complete destruction of suffering. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, how is the noble eightfold path developed and cultivated so that it leads to the complete destruction of suffering? “Bhikkhu, here a bhikkhu develops right view, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release; he develops right intention... right speech... right action... right livelihood... right effort... right mindfulness... and he develops right concentration, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that the noble eightfold path is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the complete destruction of suffering. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"For the benefit of the Vajrācārya, there is the practice of the attendant; for the illustrious Mahābhūtīs, there is the practice of the Vajrācārya. They gladden one another, and therein the bliss of the Bhūtīs arises in the mind."
Now, therefore, in the *Bhūtaḍāmara-mahātantrarāja*, there follows the detailed procedure for the accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the illustrious Mahābhūtinī.

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times before the Blessed Lord, the Glorious Sovereign of Wrath. Thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Then, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to one's means, one should burn *guggulu* incense and recite throughout the entire night. Thereupon, at dawn, she will certainly arrive. When she has arrived, an offering (*argha*) of sandalwood water should be presented, and one should say, "Welcome. She will ask, "O practitioner, what do you command? The practitioner should say, "Become my wife. She then bestows divine elixirs and rejuvenators (*rasāyana*), as well as perfected substances, kingdoms, and hidden treasures. This is the first procedure for the propitiation of the gentle [deities].
Ap 26.3 Now, furthermore, there are forceful methods (*haṭhasādhana*).

Having drawn Śrībhūtinī with saffron on birch bark, one should, being alone and naked at night, recite [the mantra] eight thousand times before the Vajradhara. She comes quickly. Once she has arrived, she should be enjoyed. She becomes pleased; she grants a kingdom; she even grants the status of Śakra. Carrying one upon her back, she leads one even to the heavenly realm. One lives for a thousand years. If it does not succeed, [her] eye and head burst, she withers, and she dies instantly.
26.4 Now, therefore, follows the detailed procedure for the rite of killing a *bhūtinī*.
As before, one should employ the incantations for killing in the center of the mandala. Within a moment, he kills the *bhūtinī*. This was spoken by Krodha himself.
Having written the name with saffron, having stepped upon it with the left foot, and brandishing the vajra while uttering "hūṃ" seven times, one certainly kills [the target] in an instant.
In the *Bhūtaḍāmaramahātantrarāja*, this is the detailed procedure for the method of accomplishment.

Having summoned the being born of the gods and prostrated before him, one should dismiss him with the mantra:
"In whatever way the great being may release the place of wrath, svāhā! This is the mantra for summoning the deities of the offering.

Having offered blood, food, flowers, and incense to the deities of the offering, and having covered the *bali* with a white cloth, one should recite this mantra three times. Having prostrated before those born of the gods, one should dismiss them.

In whatever way it may be, let the great elements go to their own respective abodes! Let them go quickly to the cremation grounds, the temples of the gods, solitary trees, riverbanks, crossroads, single lingas, or the shrines of the gods, in order to observe the covenant of the spirits (*bhūta*). If they do not go thus, he shall split their heads with the thunderbolt; in an instant he shall destroy them, and the spirits shall fall into the Raurava hell. Go to your own abodes as you please, *svāhā*!
In the *Bhūtaḍāmara-mahātantrarāja*, this is the extensive tantra on the ritual procedure for the bali offering.
